text: IPv4's 32-bit address space, about 4.3 billion addresses, was exhausted at the regional registry level years ago. IPv6 solves this with a 128-bit space — roughly 340 undecillion addresses, written as eight groups of four hex digits separated by colons.

Two shortening rules make IPv6 manageable: leading zeros in each group can be dropped, and one run of consecutive all-zero groups can be replaced with a double colon — but only once per address, since using it twice would make the address ambiguous.

Unicast addresses identify a single interface. Multicast addresses, always starting with ff00::/8, identify a group of interfaces. Link-local addresses, always starting with fe80::/10, are self-assigned on every IPv6 interface and never routed beyond the local segment.

The most important difference from IPv4: IPv6 has no broadcast address at all. Anything IPv4 did with broadcast — ARP requests, DHCP discovery — IPv6 does with multicast instead, sent only to the specific group of interfaces that actually need it, a deliberate efficiency improvement.

IPv6 is increasingly the default on modern operating systems, often running alongside IPv4 even on networks that don't intentionally use it — a security control built only around IPv4 can leave an entire IPv6 path unmonitored, which is exactly why recognizing fe80:: and ff00:: on sight matters for a SOC analyst.
